title: We Solve the Same Problems. We Just Use Different Words.
text:
I’ve spent most of my career trying to answer some version of the same question: why do outcomes differ across people, and can we actually trust the data telling us that they do?
That’s the center of epidemiology. But it also shows up constantly in product, strategy, evaluation, analytics, and basically anywhere decisions depend on drawing reliable conclusions from messy data.
A lot of those questions are ones epidemiologists are trained to answer. We just use different words for them.
Here are a few examples.







Practical question
Epidemiologic translation




Did the campaign work?
Did the exposure cause the outcome?


These two things move together. Does one cause the other?
Is the association confounded?


Why does this work better for some groups?
Is there effect modification?


Can we trust this metric?
Is this measure valid?


Are the people giving us feedback representative?
Is there selection bias?


Who is likely to churn, convert, or become high-cost?
Who is at risk?


What meaningful groups exist?
Are there latent subpopulations?





Did the campaign work?
Before giving credit to an intervention, you have to rule out everything else that changed at the same time. Sales went up, but was that the campaign? Or was it seasonality, or a competitor who exited the market?
An epidemiologist would ask, what would have happened if the intervention never occurred?
Difference-in-differences · Interrupted time series


These two things move together. Does one cause the other?
Association is often the start of the analysis, not the conclusion.
Customers who use a feature may spend more, but they may also have been more engaged before they ever used it. People who exercise more may also have higher incomes, better access to healthcare, and healthier diets.
A third factor can make two things appear connected even when one is not driving the other.
Confounding assessment · Causal inference · Sensitivity analysis


Why does this work better for some groups than others?
An average effect can hide everything interesting. The same product, campaign, or policy can work differently depending on who is receiving it, and sometimes that variation is the finding.
Knowing who it works for is often more useful than knowing whether it works on average.
Interaction terms · Stratified analyses


Can we trust this metric?
Before acting on a measure, it’s worth asking how it was constructed, what it captures, and what it might be excluding.
The same question applies whether you’re looking at a customer satisfaction score or a disease surveillance system.
Validation studies · Measurement error assessment


Are the people giving us feedback representative?
The people in your data are not necessarily representative of the people you care about.
People who respond to a survey differ from people who don’t. Early adopters differ from later users. People who seek out a service differ from those who never enter the system.
A big source of bias is often who we’re missing.
Selection bias · Weighting · Missing data methods


Who is most likely to churn, convert, or become high-cost?
Many decisions depend on identifying who is most likely to experience an event before it happens and understanding what predicts that transition.
The outcome is different depending on the industry, but the problems and how we solve them are the same.
Risk prediction · Survival analysis · Longitudinal modeling


What meaningful groups exist?
People don’t behave as one homogeneous group, and they don’t always sort neatly into the categories we’d expect.
Sometimes the most useful insight comes from identifying groups of people who share patterns of behavior, attitudes, or needs, especially when those groups don’t map onto obvious demographic categories.

Latent class analysis · Clustering

Epidemiology is technically the study of disease distribution and determinants in populations. But in practice, it’s a set of tools for figuring out why outcomes differ and whether what you’re seeing is real.
Those tools travel.

title: Precious Esie, PhD
text:
About
My name is Precious, and I’m a quantitative researcher trained in social epidemiology. My work focuses on using population and behavioral data to understand why outcomes differ across people and places.
I studied mathematics as an undergraduate, which trained me to think through hard problems. Epidemiology gave me a way to apply that way of thinking to questions about health, behavior, and the social conditions people live in. Across different topics, I’ve stayed interested in the same underlying challenge of figuring out what the data we have can tell us about why outcomes differ, and for whom.
I’m drawn to problems that call for methods like causal inference, behavioral segmentation, longitudinal modeling, spatial analysis, or other approaches that help make sense of population data. My experience spans academic, government, and applied research settings, including the CDC’s Epidemic Intelligence Service and Microsoft Research. I have 18 peer-reviewed publications, including 9 as first author, in outlets including the American Journal of Public Health and MMWR.
Outside of work, I’m a distance runner training for my third marathon. I enjoy growing things on my balcony, drinking cold brew with oat milk, and spending more time than I should building Spotify playlists that follow music backwards through samples and influences.


Background
PhD, Epidemiology — Columbia University, 2022
MPH, Epidemiology — Emory University, 2016
BS, Mathematics — Loyola University New Orleans, 2013
Currently based in Atlanta, GA.
View my publications →

I use population and behavioral data to make sense of why outcomes differ across people and places.
I’m a quantitative researcher trained in social epidemiology. Across different topics and settings, I’ve stayed interested in the same challenge of figuring out what imperfect data can tell us about the world.
More about me →



How I Work
I start by understanding what decision the analysis is meant to inform. Before running models, I examine where the data came from and what assumptions are built into it. Some questions require causal methods. Others are better answered with segmentation, a descriptive analysis, or a clear chart. Results rarely speak for themselves, so part of the work is translating findings into language that supports decisions while being honest about what the data can and cannot support.


Selected Work

Using nationally representative survey data, this analysis identifies four ways people navigate health information and examines how those differences relate to trust and perceived care quality.

title: Trust and Quality of Care Depend on How People Experience Health Information
text:
I’ve done segmentation work in health contexts where the goal is behavior change. That work kept raising the same problem — demographics can describe who people are, but they rarely explain what would actually help them.
That gap is especially relevant to health information. Public health efforts often assume that if accurate information is available, people will know what to do with it. But many people are navigating a constant stream of recommendations, warnings, and advice that is difficult to make sense of, especially when messages seem to conflict or change over time.
The scale of that difficulty is visible in the data. In 2024, about 70% of U.S. adults said health recommendations from experts seem to change often. Nearly three-quarters said there are so many recommendations about preventing cancer that it is hard to know which ones to follow.
These are not fringe views. They are the dominant experience.
The Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) offers a way to examine that experience. HINTS is a nationally representative survey from the National Cancer Institute that asks U.S. adults about health information seeking, cancer-related knowledge and behaviors, provider communication, source trust, and health information use.
The survey includes several questions about what it feels like to navigate health recommendations. Looking at those questions, two themes emerged: whether expert guidance seems inconsistent or contradictory, and whether the volume of recommendations feels overwhelming. Although these experiences may seem similar, they are not necessarily the same thing. Someone can trust experts but still feel overwhelmed by the volume of information. Others may feel less burdened by volume but question the consistency of what they hear.
A factor analysis supported that distinction, where inconsistency and overload reflect separate dimensions of how people experience health information.
Expert inconsistency (do recommendations contradict or change):

How often health recommendations from experts seem to change over time
How often health recommendations from experts seem to contradict each other

Information overload (are there too many recommendations):

Whether there are so many different recommendations about preventing cancer, it’s hard to know which ones to follow
Whether it feels like everything causes cancer


Four profiles emerged from the data
I then used latent class analysis to identify whether people clustered into distinct profiles based on these responses. Among 6,435 U.S. adults, four profiles emerged.
The profiles are not driven by demographics. Age, education, race, and income vary only slightly across groups. What separates them is how they experience the information environment.

People who struggle with health information trust the system less and rate their care lower
The four groups differed substantially in both trust and perceived care quality, and the pattern runs in one direction where more difficulty navigating health information is associated with lower trust and worse care experiences.
People in Class 1, who reported the lowest levels of both inconsistency and overload, had the highest trust across every measure. More than 80% trusted doctors a lot, about half trusted the healthcare system a lot, and over one-quarter rated their care as excellent.
People in Class 4, who reported high levels of both, were at the other end on every outcome. Trust in the healthcare system was roughly half the rate seen in Class 1, and fewer than one in five rated their care as excellent.
The largest group, Class 2, fell in between. These adults reported feeling overwhelmed by health information but did not perceive expert guidance as contradictory or unstable. Their trust levels were lower than Class 1 but higher than Classes 3 and 4, which suggests that volume alone is not the main driver of distrust.

Most people feel overwhelmed. Fewer perceive conflicting guidance. Both matter.
Information overload is the more common experience. Nearly six in ten adults fall into one of the high overload groups, Classes 2 and 4. Perceived inconsistency is less common, about three in ten adults fall into one of the high inconsistency groups, Classes 3 and 4.
For medical institutions, inconsistency appears more strongly tied to distrust. Compared with adults in the low overload, low inconsistency group, trust in the healthcare system was 7 percentage points lower among those with high overload but low inconsistency, and 17 percentage points lower among those with low overload but high inconsistency. A similar pattern holds for trust in doctors.
For government and scientists, neither overload nor inconsistency alone stood out. Both were associated with drops of roughly similar size. But looking at the combination, people with high levels of both reported trust gaps that were larger than either factor would suggest on its own.
Perceived care quality shows this most clearly. High overload alone was associated with almost no difference in ratings, and high inconsistency alone wasn’t much different. But people experiencing both rated their care substantially worse than any other group, suggesting the two experiences together produce something the individual pieces don’t.

Clearer explanations of why recommendations change, and how to act when they appear to conflict.

What this can and can’t tell us
This is a cross-sectional study. It can show that these profiles exist and that they differ on outcomes that matter. It cannot show whether high information overload causes lower trust or lower perceived care quality, or whether people who already struggle with health information are more likely to feel overwhelmed. The arrow of causation is not visible here.
That said, the analysis suggests that people’s experiences of the health information environment vary in meaningful ways, are associated with trust and perceived care quality, and are not captured by demographic characteristics alone.

B. Variable selection





The segmentation uses four variables from HINTS 7. Two capture perceived inconsistency: A4 (“How often do health recommendations from experts seem to conflict or contradict one another?”) and A5 (“How often do health recommendations from experts seem to change over time?”). Two capture perceived overload: P1c (“There are so many different recommendations about preventing cancer, it’s hard to know which ones to follow”) and P1a (“It seems like everything causes cancer”). Variables were selected because they directly capture how people experience the health information environment.

D. Sample





The analytic sample excludes respondents with missing data on any segmentation or profiling variable (n = 843 excluded from the raw sample of 7,278). Missingness was broadly consistent across demographic groups and across classes, suggesting limited selection bias.

title: Selected Publications
text:
For a full list, please see my Google Scholar profile →

Neighborhood Air Pollution Disparities in Chicago (2022)
American Journal of Public Health
Can low-cost sensor networks detect neighborhood-level disparities in air pollution that regulatory monitors miss? A dense sensor network deployed across Chicago found that racial and ethnic composition predicted fine particulate matter exposure at the neighborhood level, including during wildfire and July 4th episodes.


Social Vulnerability and Firearm Injury in King County, Washington (2024)
Public Health Reports
Do areas with higher social vulnerability have higher rates of firearm injury? Using EMS data and Bayesian spatial modeling across King County, Washington, this study found that high-vulnerability areas had firearm injury rates three times higher than low-vulnerability areas.


Depression Within the US Black Population (2023)
Epidemiologic Reviews
Does treating the US Black population as a single group obscure meaningful differences in depression? This review synthesized decades of research across Black ethnic and immigrant groups. It found substantial variation by nativity, region of birth, and Caribbean origin, and argued for better data collection and more precise measurement.


Sex Gaps in Cannabis Use and Cannabis Use Disorder (2025)
Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
Are sex differences in cannabis use and cannabis use disorder changing over time? Using national survey data from 2014 to 2023, this study tracked prevalence trends by sex and age group. By 2022, adolescent females had surpassed males in past-month cannabis use, a reversal of a longstanding pattern.


Intimate Partner Violence and Depression in Rural Bangladesh (2019)
SSM — Population Health
Does the severity of intimate partner violence matter for depression risk, beyond simple yes/no exposure measures? In rural Bangladesh, where IPV is endemic, this study found a clear dose-response relationship between abuse severity and major depressive episode across psychological, physical, and sexual violence.

title: Perception Is Not a Noisy Version of Reality
text:
There is a version of this problem that shows up in applied research, usually framed as a measurement quality issue. You have two measures of the same construct, one objective and one subjective. They don’t agree. Which one do you trust?
I’ve become less convinced that’s the right question.
The longer I work with behavioral data, the more I notice that perceived and objective measures often aren’t measuring the same thing at all. The choice between them is a claim about what you think is driving behavior, and from what I’ve seen, many researchers make that claim without knowing it.

The assumption hidden inside measurement
In conversations about perceived versus objective measures, I’ve noticed how quickly the discussion turns to accuracy. Is one more biased? Is one easier to defend? Those questions matter, but they can also make it sound as if both measures are aiming at the same target.
Sometimes they are. A self-reported diagnosis and a medical record diagnosis may both be attempts to capture the presence of the same condition.
But some constructs don’t work that way. A person’s perception of safety is related to local conditions, but it’s also shaped by their own experiences, what they’ve seen happen to people they know, and what they believe could happen to them. There’s no external record that tells you which of those inputs is wrong. Perception isn’t inherently a flawed estimate of the crime rate. It may be capturing something the crime rate can’t.


Consider the discordant cases
Take two people living in the same neighborhood. The available objective indicators are the same — the same recorded crime rate, the same sidewalks, the same lighting, the same local resources. But subjective measures differ. One feels safe walking alone at night, the other does not.
The person who feels unsafe may avoid walking outside, limit contact with neighbors, or underuse local resources, regardless of what crime statistics say. In that case, perceived safety is not a weaker version of the objective measure. It may be closer to the mechanism you are actually trying to understand.
This is why the discordant cases are worth paying attention to. When someone perceives high risk despite low objective risk, or strong social support despite weak objective support, it forces a different question. Not which measure is correct, but which measure is most relevant to the mechanism you care about.


Measurement choices are causal claims
Every measure implies a theory. If you believe behavior changes mainly because objective conditions change, it makes sense to measure those conditions directly. If you believe behavior changes because people perceive those conditions differently, then perception belongs in the model. An intervention that changes objective conditions without touching perception may not move behavior at all, and if you never measured perception, you won’t know why.

  Path A — direct
  
    Objective conditions
    
      
    
    Behavior
  
  
  Path B — mediated
  
    Objective conditions
    
      
    
    Perception
    
      
    
    Behavior
  
  
    If Path B is closer to the mechanism and you only measure Path A, you may misread your results and not know why.
  



I’m not saying objective measures are suspect or that perception always wins. Sometimes objective conditions shape perception in ways that make the distinction less clean than it looks on paper. But the choice should follow from an explicit theory of the mechanism, not from a default preference for data that feels more concrete. Objectivity is not the same as validity. A measure is valid when it captures the construct that’s causally relevant to the outcome you’re studying. Sometimes that construct is a perception.


Before choosing a measure
Rather than asking which measure is more accurate, it may be worth asking: what has to change for the behavior I care about to change?
For some questions, the answer points toward objective conditions. For others, it points toward how people are interpreting those conditions. If you’re not sure which path is operating, that’s worth figuring out.
The measure you choose does more than describe the world. It reveals what part of the world you think matters.
